original_question: Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable? See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57.
target_in_paper: Problem 21.73 in the 21st issue (New Problems, 2026): "Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable? See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57."
correct_elements: Your draft captures the exact target problem essentially verbatim: it asks about algorithmic decidability of the conjugacy problem in the correct group, CT(Z), and it correctly points to 17.57 for the needed definition.
missing_details: It is not stand-alone, because it refers externally to 17.57 instead of defining CT(Z).
It omits the notation r(m) = {r + km | k ∈ Z} for integers m >= 1 and 0 <= r < m.
It omits that a class transposition is defined only for disjoint residue classes r1(m1) and r2(m2).
It omits the exact action of the class transposition τ_{r1(m1),r2(m2)}: for every k ∈ Z it swaps r1 + km1 with r2 + km2 and fixes every other integer.
It omits that CT(Z) is the subgroup of Sym(Z) generated by all such class transpositions.
It leaves implicit that the conjugacy is internal to CT(Z): given g,h ∈ CT(Z), decide whether there exists x ∈ CT(Z) with xgx^{-1} = h.

For an algorithmic question, the input representation should be stated explicitly; the natural paper-faithful encoding is that g and h are given as finite words (finite products) in class transpositions.
refined_question: Let r(m) = {r + km | k ∈ Z} for integers m >= 1 and 0 <= r < m. If r1(m1) ∩ r2(m2) = ∅, let τ_{r1(m1),r2(m2)} be the involution of Z that swaps r1 + km1 with r2 + km2 for every k ∈ Z and fixes every other integer. Let CT(Z) be the subgroup of Sym(Z) generated by all such class transpositions. Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable; that is, given two elements g,h ∈ CT(Z), each specified as a finite word in class transpositions, is there an algorithm to decide whether there exists x ∈ CT(Z) such that xgx^{-1} = h?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 21.73. Problem 17.57 supplies the notation for residue classes, the definition of class transpositions, and the definition of CT(Z). So the paper-faithful refinement is not to broaden or alter the problem, but simply to inline the 17.57 definition and make the decision-problem input/output explicit.
